extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy; readers of Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the normative criteria Plato gives for philosophers, guardians, and rulers in the Republic (Books V–VI). Focuses on the qualities, behaviours, and institutional prescriptions that define a true philosopher-ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between war and discord
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is a difference in the names ‘discord’ and ‘war,’ and I imagine that there is also a difference in their natures; the one is expressive of what is internal and domestic, the other of what is external and foreign.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conceptual distinction to judge conduct between compatriots versus foreigners: intra-polis strife should be treated as discord (a quarrel among friends) not war; responses should avoid total devastation or treating the whole population as enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on plunder in intra-Hellenic conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Both should be forbidden, in my judgment; I would take the annual produce and no more.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conflict is internal (discord), take only limited recompense (annual produce); do not devastate lands or burn houses. This is presented as a moral/legal constraint on conduct toward kinsmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on devastation and burning for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Then let us enact this law also for our guardians:—that they are neither to devastate the lands of Hellenes nor to burn their houses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concrete legislative prescription: guardians (rulers/defenders) must not raze or burn citizens' homes nor devastate allied/native lands—policy for humane internal governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal as heuristic; approximation acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The project is to create an ideal of a perfect State and of absolute justice not necessarily to prove its full historical realization: 'we were to look at these in order that we might judge of our own happiness... but not with any view of showing that they could exist in fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing reforms or ideals, it suffices to show how a close approximation might be realized; one need not prove the ideal exists in full. Use the ideal as a measuring standard rather than a literal program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers as rulers (primary political reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy... cities will never have rest from their evils.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's fundamental political criterion: stability and justice require rulers who possess philosophical wisdom. Evaluate regimes by whether political authority is exercised by those with philosophical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher as lover of the whole of wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The philosopher... is a lover, not of a part of wisdom only, but of the whole.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true philosophers from partial lovers (of music, sights, honours): a true philosopher desires comprehensive knowledge, not merely specialized or sensual pleasures masquerading as wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge vs opinion (subject-matter distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The mind of the one who knows has knowledge, and that of the other, who opines only, has opinion... Being is the sphere or subject-matter of knowledge... opinion is intermediate.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the epistemic distinction to assess claims and disputants: knowledge concerns the immutable (being), opinion concerns the intermediate/variable. Rulers should be guided by knowledge, not opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and hatred of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Truthfulness: they will never intentionally receive into their mind falsehood, which is their detestation, and they will love the truth.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A necessary moral quality: philosophers must actively reject deliberate falsehood. In evaluating a leader or thinker, check for habitual commitment to truth over expedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and lack of covetousness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He whose desires are drawn towards knowledge in every form will... hardly feel bodily pleasure—I mean, if he be a true philosopher and not a sham one... sure to be temperate and the reverse of covetous.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical character implies self-control and indifference to wealth/pleasure; absence of covetousness is a sign of authenticity. Anti-pattern: those who pursue honours or possessions rather than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of mind; absence of meanness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There should be no secret corner of illiberality; nothing can be more antagonistic than meanness to a soul which is ever longing after the whole of things both divine and human.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true philosopher has grandeur of spirit—generosity of outlook and refusal of petty or mean concerns. Evaluate by openness, magnanimity, and concern for large things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and fearlessness of death
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Or can such an one account death fearful? No indeed. Then the cowardly and mean nature has no part in true philosophy.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical courage: absence of irrational fear, including fear of death. Use readiness to face danger in defense of truth/justice as an indicator of genuine philosophical temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice, gentleness and sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Can he... ever be unjust or hard in his dealings? Impossible. Then you will soon observe whether a man is just and gentle, or rude and unsociable; these are the signs which distinguish...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpersonal virtues—justice and gentleness—are diagnostic of the philosophical soul. Rudeness and unsociability point away from true philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in learning and retention (good memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whether he has or has not a pleasure in learning... if he is forgetful and retains nothing of what he learns, will he not be an empty vessel?... we must insist that the philosopher should have a good memory.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine philosopher delights in learning and remembers what is learned. Assess candidates by curiosity, sustained engagement with learning, and ability to retain and use knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-proportioned, harmonious mind
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We must try to find a naturally well-proportioned and gracious mind, which will move spontaneously towards the true being of everything.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal philosopher has internal harmony and proportion (lack of inharmonious dispositions). Look for balanced character, aesthetic and moral proportion as indicators of fitness to rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of intellectual and moral excellences for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Those in whom they are united, and those only, should be rulers in the State.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulership requires both philosophical knowledge and moral virtues (courage, temperance, justice). Evaluate leaders on both axes—technical wisdom and moral character—not one alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence over popularity (pilot/ship parable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parable: the true pilot must know navigation, attend to sky and stars and seasons, and will be the steerer whether other people like or not; mutinous sailors who claim the helm without skill are dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional criterion: entrust governance to those with the relevant art/skill (knowledge of the good), not to noisy or popular claimants. Anti-pattern: leaders who claim authority without training and call experts 'star-gazers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers' public uselessness is social, not personal
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘They are quite right’ in thinking many philosophers useless, but blame lies with those who will not use them: the true helmsmen are ignored or mistreated by the mutinous sailors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the social role of philosophers, distinguish between philosophers' actual capacities and the society's failure to employ their skills; social marginalization is not proof of incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical striving after being (intellectual vocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The true lover of knowledge is always striving after being—that is his nature;... he will not rest in the multiplicity of individuals... until he have attained the knowledge of the true nature of every essence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess philosophical authenticity by the depth and relentless character of inquiry—persistent movement toward understanding essences rather than settling for appearances or facile explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as captain bringing justice and health of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When truth is the captain, we cannot suspect any evil of the band which he leads... Justice and health of mind will be of the company, and temperance will follow after.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: if governance is guided by truth, moral goods (justice, temperance, mental health) naturally accompany it. Use the presence of these collective goods as evidence that truth is guiding policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of natural gifts associated with the philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Courage, magnificence, apprehension, memory’ are cited as the philosopher's natural gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging individuals for philosophical or ruling roles, look for this cluster of native capacities (courage, grandeur, quick apprehension, memory) supplemented by education and years of formation.
